claim: P300 is one of the most extensively investigated evoked responses (ER) in electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG).
source: P300 is one of the most extensively investigated evoked responses (ER) in electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG).
evidence: This is a general statement about the prominence of P300 in the literature, supported by the extensive citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: P300 has been hypothesised to reflect a variety of functions, such as priming, cognitive processing, memory storage, context updating, and resource allocation.
source: Over the years, P300 has been hypothesised to reflect a variety of functions, such as priming, cognitive processing, memory storage, context updating, resource allocation, etc. (Polich and Kok, 1995; Polich, 2003; Verleger, 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Polich and Kok, 1995; Polich, 2003; Verleger, 2020).

claim: P300 is usually assessed with the oddball paradigm where participants detect a target stimulus in a train of standard stimuli.
source: Usually, P300 is assessed with the oddball paradigm (auditory or visual), where participants have a task to detect a target (or rare, or deviant) stimulus in a train of standard (or frequent, or non-target) stimuli (Luck, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Luck, 2014, and represents established methodological knowledge.

claim: The P300 complex involves the earlier frontal component P3a and the later parietal component P3b.
source: Additionally, it is usual to speak about the P300 complex, involving the earlier frontal component P3a and the later parietal component P3b (Linden, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Linden, 2005.

claim: The exact mechanism of P300 generation remains rather unknown.
source: Adding to the complexity of P300, the exact mechanism of P300 generation remains rather unknown (Fell et al., 2004; Hanslmayr et al., 2007; Daly et al., 2009; Rawls et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations indicating ongoing uncertainty in the field.

claim: The oddball target stimulus concurrently causes the attenuation of the alpha rhythm amplitude (8–12 Hz).
source: Apart from P300, the oddball target stimulus concurrently causes the attenuation of the alpha rhythm amplitude (8–12 Hz).
evidence: This is a statement about the empirical observation that is supported by the extensive literature review in Appendix 1.

claim: The simultaneity of P300 and alpha rhythm modulation has been observed in numerous earlier and more recent studies.
source: The simultaneity of P300 and alpha rhythm modulation has been observed in numerous earlier and more recent studies, and in Appendix 1 we offer a short overview of these findings.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Appendix 1 which contains a literature review.

claim: 38 studies presented results for a concomitant occurrence of P300 and alpha power (or amplitude).
source: We found 38 studies that presented results for a concomitant occurrence of P300 and alpha power (or amplitude).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the literature review conducted by the authors.

claim: In 17 EEG studies, results indicated an overlap in cortical regions of P300 and alpha amplitude decrease, as well as similar time windows of their occurrence.
source: In 17 studies using EEG, results indicated an overlap in cortical regions of P300 and alpha amplitude decrease, as well as a similar time windows of their occurrence (Peng et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2015; Shou and Ding, 2015; Tang et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2015; Fabi and Leuthold, 2017; López-Caneda et al., 2017; Vilà-Balló et al., 2017; Fabi and Leuthold, 2018; Michelini et al., 2018; Román-López et al., 2019; Kao et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020; Nikolin et al., 2021; Paolicelli et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to 17 specific studies.

claim: Similar observations of P300 and alpha amplitude overlap were made using MEG.
source: Similar observations were made using MEG (Ishii et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ishii et al., 2009.

claim: Yordanova et al., 2001 and 14 more studies found similarities in location but not in the peak latencies between P300 and alpha modulation.
source: Yordanova et al., 2001 and 14 more studies found similarities in location but not in the peak latencies (Kolev et al., 2001; Kamarajan et al., 2006; Digiacomo et al., 2008; Krämer et al., 2011; Barutchu et al., 2013; Deiber et al., 2013; Kayser et al., 2014; Zarka et al., 2014; Deiber et al., 2015; Leroy et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2019; Martel et al., 2019; Faro et al., 2019; Espenhahn et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to 15 specific studies.

claim: In a few studies, alpha modulation did not appear at all or the relationship between alpha oscillations and ER was not supported by cross-condition comparison.
source: In a few studies, alpha modulation did not appear at all (Kamarajan et al., 2004; Delval et al., 2018) or the relationship between alpha oscillations and ER was not supported by cross-condition comparison (Cooper et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2017; Tamura et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to specific studies that found contrary results.

claim: The baseline-shift mechanism (BSM) links evoked activity and spontaneous oscillatory activity, stating that if oscillations are modulated by the stimulus presentation, this modulation will be mirrored in the low-frequency signal if oscillations have a non-zero mean.
source: In general theory, BSM links evoked activity and spontaneous oscillatory activity, stating that if oscillations are modulated by the stimulus presentation, this modulation will be mirrored in the low-frequency signal if oscillations have a non-zero mean (see Figure 1).
evidence: The claim describes the theoretical basis of BSM and references Figure 1 for illustration.

claim: The amplitude modulation of the oscillatory process affects the mean, which leads to deflection in the spectral range of modulation activity.
source: In other words, the amplitude modulation of the oscillatory process affects the mean as well, which in turn leads to the deflection in the spectral range of modulation activity (with the frequency of modulation lying in a considerably lower range than the carrier frequency of oscillations themselves; for instance, if the oscillations' frequency range is 8–12 Hz, the modulation's frequency range is 0–3 Hz).
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism based on theoretical understanding.

claim: When integrated over several periods, oscillations with a non-zero mean will show an average value different from zero that will scale with the amplitude of oscillations.
source: In practice, when integrated over several periods, oscillations with a non-zero mean will show an average value different from zero that will scale with the amplitude of oscillations.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of BSM.

claim: A non-zero mean implies that average values of the upper and lower half of the oscillatory cycle would be unequal.
source: Likewise, a non-zero mean implies that average values of the upper and lower half of the oscillatory cycle would be unequal.
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of having a non-zero mean.

claim: Negative-mean oscillations undergoing a decrease in amplitude create an ER with positive polarity according to BSM.
source: In Figure 1, negative-mean oscillations undergo a decrease in the amplitude in the poststimulus window and, according to BSM, the decrease in the amplitude of negative-mean oscillations creates an ER with a positive polarity.
evidence: This is a prediction of BSM illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The polarity of the ER depends on the sign of the oscillatory mean and on the direction of modulation.
source: The polarity of the ER depends on the sign of the oscillatory mean and on the direction of modulation—an increase or decrease in the amplitude.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of BSM.

claim: The oscillatory mean of alpha oscillations has been shown to be present in biophysical model of alpha oscillations.
source: The oscillatory mean of alpha oscillations has been shown to be present in biophysical model of alpha oscillations (Studenova et al., 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Studenova et al., 2022.

claim: Several studies provided empirical evidence for the generation of ER through BSM in somatosensory and visual domains.
source: and several studies provided empirical evidence for the generation of ER through BSM in somatosensory (Nikulin et al., 2007) and visual (Mazaheri and Jensen, 2008; Iemi et al., 2019) domain.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Average time courses of P300 and alpha amplitude envelope demonstrate an inverse relation—while P300 has a positive deflection, alpha rhythm amplitude is attenuated.
source: In line with the first prediction, average time courses of P300 and alpha amplitude envelope demonstrate an inverse relation—while P300 has a positive deflection, alpha rhythm amplitude is attenuated (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Within a window 200–400ms after stimulus onset, P300 has a rising flank and alpha amplitude starts to decrease.
source: More specifically, within a window 200–400ms after stimulus onset, P300 has a rising flank and alpha amplitude starts to decrease, and within a window 400–700ms, both P300 and alpha amplitude have the largest magnitude (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Within a window 400–700ms, both P300 and alpha amplitude have the largest magnitude.
source: More specifically, within a window 200–400ms after stimulus onset, P300 has a rising flank and alpha amplitude starts to decrease, and within a window 400–700ms, both P300 and alpha amplitude have the largest magnitude (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The correlation between P300 and alpha amplitude envelope for the target stimulus was significantly negative at posterior regions, with correlation of –0.86 at Pz.
source: As predicted, the correlation for the target stimulus was significantly negative at posterior regions (Figure 2C, at Pz correlation is –0.86).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis presented in Figure 2C.

claim: When alpha amplitude envelopes were sorted into 5 bins according to normalized change, the P300 amplitude followed the partition of alpha amplitudes.
source: Indeed, when we sorted alpha amplitude envelopes between participants into 5 bins according to the normalised change, the P300 amplitude followed the partition of alpha amplitudes.
evidence: The claim is supported by the binning analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: For participants with a stronger alpha amplitude modulation, the amplitude of P300 was higher than for participants with weak amplitude modulation.
source: The different alpha amplitude dynamics correlated with P300 amplitude, such that for participants with a stronger alpha amplitude modulation, the amplitude of P300 was higher than for participants with weak amplitude modulation (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The t-test between the most extreme bins demonstrates a significant spatio-temporal cluster in the posterior region spanning electrodes CP6, P3, P4, P7, Pz, O1, O2, PO9.
source: The t-test between the most extreme bins demonstrates a significant spatio-temporal cluster in the posterior region spanning electrodes CP6, P3, P4, P7, Pz, O1, O2, PO9 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Spatial distributions of P300 and alpha amplitude modulation overlapped considerably with Spearman correlation between topographies of –0.80.
source: Consistently with the second prediction, spatial distributions of P300 and alpha amplitude modulation overlapped considerably (Spearman correlation between topographies –0.80, p-value <0.0001, Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis and data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The highest amplitude of P300 is localised over posterior electrodes.
source: The highest amplitude of P300 (as contrasted with sER) is localised over posterior electrodes.
evidence: The claim is supported by the topographical analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The highest alpha amplitude change appears in the same posterior region as P300.
source: Similarly, the highest alpha amplitude change (also contrasted with alpha amplitude after standard stimulus) appears in the same region.
evidence: The claim is supported by the topographical analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The topographies were sampled at the peak of P300, which on average happened at 509±171ms after the stimulus onset.
source: The topographies were sampled at the peak of P300, which on average happened at 509±171ms after the stimulus onset.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the data analysis.

claim: The biggest activations for both ER and alpha amplitude were localised on the parietal midline (precuneus, posterior cingulate cortex, BA 7, 31, 23).
source: The biggest activations for both ER and alpha amplitude were localised on the parietal midline (precuneus, posterior cingulate cortex, BA 7, 31, 23; Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by source reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The location of P300 is compatible with previous studies.
source: The location of P300 is compatible with previous studies (Tarkka et al., 1996; Tarkka and Stokic, 1998; Faro et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The BSIs tended to be negative on average at Pz and in the nearby occipital region.
source: The BSIs tended to be negative on average at Pz and in the nearby occipital region (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The distribution of BSIs at Pz was skewed towards negative values, with a mean value of −0.12 and a mode of −0.85.
source: The distribution of BSIs at Pz was skewed towards negative values (Figure 6B), with a mean value of −0.12 and a mode of −0.85.
evidence: The claim is supported by descriptive statistics from the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The distribution of BSIs had a trough around zero, which indicates that oscillatory activity more often was a non-zero mean.
source: The distribution had a trough around zero, which indicates that oscillatory activity more often was a non-zero mean.
evidence: This is an inference from the distribution pattern observed in the data.

claim: At Pz, the BSI covaried with P300 amplitude such that more negative BSIs corresponded to higher amplitudes of P300 in accordance with BSM.
source: At Pz, the BSI covaried with P300 amplitude in a way that more negative BSIs corresponded to higher amplitudes of P300 in accordance with BSM, and more positive BSIs were associated with smaller amplitudes (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Significant clusters of BSI-P300 relationship were found spanning electrodes FC5, C3, C4, CP5, CP6, P3, P4, P7, P8, Pz, O1, O2, PO9, PO10, and the time window of approximately 300–700ms.
source: This trend is observed in other posterior and central electrodes (Figure 6D), and we estimated significant clusters spanning electrodes FC5, C3, C4, CP5, CP6, P3, P4, P7, P8, Pz, O1, O2, PO9, PO10, and the time window of maximal P300 amplitude, approximately 300–700ms (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Both P300 and alpha latency, but not amplitude, significantly correlated with attention scores.
source: Following this procedure, both P300 and alpha latency, but not amplitude, significantly correlated with attention scores (Figure 7A, left column).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Larger latencies were related to lower attentional scores, which corresponded to a longer time-to-complete of TMT and Stroop tests and hence poorer performance.
source: Larger latencies were related to lower attentional scores, which corresponded to a longer time-to-complete of TMT and Stroop tests and hence poorer performance.
evidence: The claim is supported by the correlation analysis with cognitive test data.

claim: The proportion of correlation between P300 latency and attention, mediated by alpha attenuation peak latency, is 0.12.
source: The proportion of correlation between P300 latency and attention, mediated by alpha attenuation peak latency, is 0.12.
evidence: This is a result from mediation analysis.

claim: Memory scores were positively related to P300 amplitude and negatively to P300 latency.
source: Memory scores were positively related to P300 amplitude and negatively to P300 latency (Figure 7A, middle column).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Higher memory scores, which reflected more recalled items, corresponded to a higher P300 amplitude and an earlier P300 peak.
source: The direction of correlation is such that higher memory scores, which reflected more recalled items, corresponded to a higher P300 amplitude and an earlier P300 peak.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation results with memory test data.

claim: Executive function was related significantly to both P300 and alpha amplitude latencies.
source: Executive function (Figure 7A, right column) were related significantly to both P300 and alpha amplitude latencies.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The proportion of correlation between P300 latency and executive function, mediated by alpha attenuation peak latency, is 0.14.
source: The proportion of correlation between P300 latency and attention, mediated by alpha attenuation peak latency, is 0.14.
evidence: This is a result from mediation analysis.

claim: The direction of correlation between cognitive scores and EEG measures is similar for P300 and alpha oscillations, as expected for BSM.
source: Overall, the direction of correlation is similar for P300 and alpha oscillations, as expected for BSM.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the correlation analyses.

claim: The direction of correlation between cognitive scores and EEG measures is consistent across cognitive functions.
source: Moreover, the direction of correlation is consistent across cognitive functions.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the correlation analyses across different cognitive domains.

claim: All four prerequisites for BSM were validated in the study: temporal similarity, spatial similarity, sign of oscillatory mean, and cognitive correlations.
source: All the required prerequisites were confirmed: (1) the temporal courses of P300 and alpha amplitude were matching, (2) the spatial topographies of the P300 component and alpha oscillations were considerably overlapping, (3) the sign of the mean of alpha oscillations determined the direction of P300 given the decrease in alpha amplitude, (4) cognitive scores correlated in a similar way with the parameters of P300 and alpha amplitude.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: P300, at least to some degree, is generated as a consequence of stimulus-triggered modulation of alpha oscillations with a non-zero mean.
source: Therefore, P300, at least to some degree, is generated as a consequence of stimulus-triggered modulation of alpha oscillations with a non-zero mean.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the validation of all four BSM prerequisites.

claim: The study used a large EEG data set from 2230 elderly participants aged 60–82 years old.
source: To validate these predictions, we analysed the data set of elderly participants (N=2230, 60–82 years old)
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: The experimental task was an auditory oddball paradigm where target tones occurred in only 12% of trials.
source: In this data set, the experimental task was an auditory oddball paradigm. Participants would hear tones, one type of which—the target tone—would occur in only 12% of trials.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Target tones elicit both P300 and the modulation of the alpha amplitude.
source: Target tones elicit both P300 and the modulation of the alpha amplitude.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The baseline-shift index (BSI) serves as a proxy for the relation between ER polarity and the direction of alpha amplitude change.
source: BSI serves as a proxy for the relation between ER polarity and the direction of alpha amplitude change (Nikulin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation to Nikulin et al., 2010.

claim: Predominantly negative BSIs at posterior sites indicate the inverted relation between P300 and alpha amplitude change.
source: Here, we observe predominantly negative BSIs (and thus negative mean oscillations) at posterior sites, which indicates the inverted relation between P300 and alpha amplitude change.
evidence: This is an inference from the BSI data based on BSM theory.

claim: A positive deflection of P300 at posterior sites coincides with a decrease in alpha amplitude.
source: Indeed, in the task data, a positive deflection of P300 at posterior sites coincides with a decrease in alpha amplitude.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: P300 has been previously associated with attention, memory, and executive function.
source: P300 is hypothesised to reflect attention, memory manipulation, and/or decision-making (Polich, 2007; Verleger, 2020), and previous studies showed that P300 correlated with attention (Becker and Shapiro, 1980; Nakajima and Imamura, 2000; Lakey et al., 2011), memory (Watter et al., 2001; Braverman and Blum, 2003; Amin et al., 2015), and executive function (Kindermann et al., 2000; Dichter et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Alpha rhythm has been linked to attention and memory.
source: Alpha rhythm has been linked to attention (Klimesch, 1999; Thut et al., 2006; Wislowska et al., 2022) and memory (Klimesch et al., 1997; Fellinger et al., 2012; van Ede, 2018; Wislowska et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The mediation analysis showed that the modulation of alpha oscillations only partially explained the correlation between P300 and cognitive variables.
source: The mediation analysis showed that the modulation of alpha oscillations only partially explained the correlation between P300 and cognitive variables.
evidence: This is a result from the mediation analysis.

claim: Not the whole P300 but only its fraction can be explained by the changes in the alpha amplitudes.
source: This, in general, corresponds to the idea that not the whole P300 but only its fraction can be explained by the changes in the alpha amplitudes.
evidence: This is an inference from the mediation analysis results.

claim: Alpha oscillations change not only in the cortical areas where P300 is generated.
source: Figure 5 shows that alpha oscillations change not only in the cortical areas where P300 is generated
evidence: This is an observation from the source reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cognitive tests and EEG recordings were performed at different time points.
source: Moreover, since cognitive tests and EEG recordings were performed at different time points, the associations between the cognitive variables and EEG markers are expected to be rather weak and to reflect only some neuronal processes common to P300, alpha rhythm, and tasks.
evidence: This is a methodological note about the study design.

claim: The majority of previous studies reveal the overlap in time windows and spatial regions of P300 and alpha amplitude decrease.
source: The majority of studies reveal the overlap in time windows and spatial regions of P300 and alpha amplitude decrease (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a summary of the literature review presented in Appendix 1.

claim: There were studies that found some discrepancies between P300 and alpha oscillations.
source: However, not all the studies observed a complete overlap in time courses, especially as alpha rhythm remained suppressed beyond the P300 window. Moreover, there were studies that found some discrepancies between P300 and alpha oscillations.
evidence: This is a summary of some contrary findings in the literature.

claim: In one study, the effects of TMS were observed only in alpha oscillations but not in P300, possibly because the TMS target did not include the P300 sources.
source: In one study (Cooper et al., 2008), the effects of TMS were observed only in alpha oscillations. Yet, the authors admitted that, possibly, the effect on P300 was not visible because the target of TMS—the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex—did not include the P300 sources.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Cooper et al., 2008 with the authors' interpretation.

claim: The evidence of the link between P300 and alpha oscillations might have been obscured in some studies due to many alpha oscillations sources being present simultaneously.
source: For other studies that failed to find the relation (Kamarajan et al., 2004; Tamura et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017; Delval et al., 2018), we hypothesise that the evidence of the link between P300 and alpha oscillations might have been obscured due to many alpha oscillations sources being present simultaneously (Rodriguez-Larios et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain discrepant findings in the literature.

claim: Due to multiple alpha sources active at the same time, it is challenging to recover the exact alpha source that was responsible for ER generation.
source: Due to multiple alpha sources active at the same time, it is challenging to recover the exact alpha source that was responsible for ER generation.
evidence: This is a methodological challenge identified by the authors.

claim: High amplitude alpha oscillations were observed in the occipital region, which is expected since participants were seated with their eyes closed.
source: In particular, we observed high amplitude alpha oscillations in the occipital region (which is expected since participants were seated with their eyes closed).
evidence: This is an observation from the data with an explanation based on established knowledge.

claim: The button press was accompanied by oscillatory changes in the alpha (mu) frequency range.
source: Moreover, the target tone presentation required participants to press the button, and as with any movement, the button press was also accompanied by oscillatory changes in the alpha (mu) frequency range (Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 1999; Nikulin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an observation from the data supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A positive correlation was found between ER and alpha amplitude envelope around C3-C4 electrodes.
source: In line with this assumption, we found a positive correlation between ER and alpha amplitude envelope around C3-C4 electrodes (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There may be a motor-related component of ER with typically observed negative polarity that may have originated from a source of alpha (mu) oscillations relating to motor activity.
source: and negative ER amplitudes over the same region (Figure 4A; also see Figure 2—figure supplement 1A where the P300 time courses have negativity over central electrodes), which indicates that, possibly, there is a motor-related component of ER (Salisbury et al., 2001), with typically observed negative polarity that may have originated from a source of alpha (mu) oscillations relating to motor activity.
evidence: This is an inference from the data supported by citation to Salisbury et al., 2001.

claim: Depending on the task, there might be other changes in rhythmic activity that occlude or completely hinder the identification of oscillations that are related to the ER in question.
source: Hence, depending on the task, there might be other changes in rhythmic activity that occlude or completely hinder the identification of oscillations that are related to the ER in question.
evidence: This is a general inference about methodological challenges.

claim: None of the previous studies explicitly tested the compliance of the P300 generation with BSM.
source: Furthermore, none of those studies explicitly tested the compliance of the P300 generation with BSM.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study based on literature review.

claim: In the same brain region, resting-state baseline shifts related to the amplitude of the non-zero mean alpha oscillations in a similar way as P300 related to stimulus-triggered alpha amplitude change.
source: In our study, we extended the analysis by showing that in the same brain region, resting-state baseline shifts related to the amplitude of the non-zero mean alpha oscillations in a similar way as P300 related to stimulus-triggered alpha amplitude change.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding of the study.

claim: When assessing the interrelatedness of ER and oscillatory processes via BSM, it is necessary to evaluate all BSM predictions.
source: It is important to note that when assessing the interrelatedness of ER and oscillatory processes via BSM, it is necessary to evaluate all BSM predictions.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation from the authors.

claim: P300 origins have been previously assessed according to the predictions of the additive mechanism and the phase-reset mechanism.
source: Previously, P300 origins have been assessed according to the predictions of the additive mechanism (Fell et al., 2004; Wan et al., 2009; Herrmann et al., 2014) and the phase-reset mechanism (Fell et al., 2004; Daly et al., 2009; Wan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research approaches supported by citations.

claim: The assessment of P300 compliance with additive and phase-reset mechanisms is rather problematic for non-invasive measures.
source: Both mechanisms have been extensively researched for different ERs, but the assessment of P300 compliance with these mechanisms is rather problematic, as is the case in general for all non-invasive measures trying to disambiguate mechanisms of ER generation (Telenczuk et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about methodological limitations supported by citation to Telenczuk et al., 2010.

claim: The additive mechanism postulates that ER is added to the overall activity and should be accompanied by an increase in total power.
source: First, the additive mechanism postulates that ER is added to the overall activity (Wood and Allison, 1981; Jervis et al., 1983; Mäkinen et al., 2005). Consequently, ER should be accompanied by an increase in total power and not only oscillatory power.
evidence: This is a description of the additive mechanism supported by citations.

claim: P300 is always accompanied by an increase in low-frequency power in the theta range, as it is its frequency range.
source: However, the P300 is always accompanied by an increase in low-frequency power in the theta range, as it is its frequency range.
evidence: This is an observation about P300 characteristics.

claim: The predicted increase in power exclusively due to the addition of activity is impossible to disentangle based on macroscopic recordings and multi-unit activity is required.
source: Therefore, the predicted increase in power exclusively due to the addition of activity (Shah et al., 2004; Mazaheri and Jensen, 2006) is impossible to disentangle based on macroscopic recordings (Telenczuk et al., 2010) and multi-unit activity is required to confirm whether an increase in power in the P300 window is of an oscillatory or non-oscillatory nature.
evidence: This is a statement about methodological limitations supported by citations.

claim: BSM can mimic the evidence for the additive mechanism, such that an ER generated via BSM will always be accompanied by a change in power in the low-frequency range.
source: Moreover, in fact, BSM can also mimic the evidence for the additive mechanism, such that an ER that is generated via BSM will always be accompanied by a change in power in the low-frequency range (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about BSM illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The phase-reset mechanism states that ER is created when a stimulus triggers the phase alignment of oscillators in a certain frequency.
source: Second, the phase-reset mechanism states that ER is created when a stimulus triggers the phase alignment of oscillators in a certain frequency (Sayers et al., 1974; Makeig et al., 2002; Hanslmayr et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the phase-reset mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Due to the frequency content of P300, there would be increased phase consistency in the theta range since ER always has phase alignment.
source: Analogously, due to the frequency content of P300, there would be increased phase consistency in the theta range since ER, be it of additive or phase-reset nature, always has phase alignment.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about expected phase consistency.

claim: Phase alignment in the poststimulus window does not contradict BSM.
source: Yet, phase alignment in the poststimulus window does not contradict BSM either.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the compatibility of observations with BSM.

claim: The current set of predictions for the additive and the phase-reset mechanism is insufficient to confirm the generation of P300 and needs further development.
source: We argue that the current set of predictions for the additive and the phase-reset mechanism is insufficient to confirm the generation of P300 and needs further development.
evidence: This is an argument made by the authors based on their analysis.

claim: All four BSM prerequisites verifiable with non-invasive EEG recordings were validated in the study.
source: As for BSM, all four BSM prerequisites (verifiable with non-invasive EEG recordings) were validated in our study, and therefore it seems reasonable to conclude that the generation of P300 is congruent with the BSM model.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings and conclusion.

claim: The evidence presented speaks for a partial rather than an exhausting explanation of P300's origin through BSM.
source: The evidence presented in the current study speaks for a partial rather than an exhausting explanation of P300's origin through BSM.
evidence: This is a qualification of the main conclusion.

claim: P300 is not a single ER but rather a complex.
source: The P300 is not a single ER but rather a complex.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: P300 was previously subdivided into P3a (earlier component around 300ms, more prominent in anterior midline) and P3b (later component with latency of 500ms and beyond, present in parietal electrodes).
source: Previously (Polich, 2003; Linden, 2005), P300 was subdivided into the complex that has an earlier component—P3a—that occurs around 300ms after stimulus onset and is more prominent in the anterior midline, and a later component—P3b—that has a latency of 500ms and beyond and is present to a large extent in the parietal electrodes.
evidence: This is a summary of previous research supported by citations.

claim: With PCA decomposition of P300, several other components have been observed, namely slow wave and very late negativity.
source: Besides, with PCA decomposition of P300, several other components have been observed, namely slow wave and very late negativity (Steiner et al., 2014)
evidence: This is a statement about P300 complexity supported by citation to Steiner et al., 2014.

claim: The known mechanisms of ER generation—additive mechanism, phase-resetting mechanism, and BSM—may explain different temporal windows of one ER.
